body_html:
On October 28, 2026, the 22,300-square-foot Trousdale Estates home once owned by Minecraft creator Markus "Notch" Persson returned to the Beverly Hills market, as reported by Canyon News. The estate sits near the top of Trousdale, trading on the two commodities that define the address: elevation and uninterrupted view. With its infinity pool framing the city grid below, the listing reads less as a single transaction than as a gauge of where the ultra-luxury Westside market sits in late 2026.

What makes Trousdale Estates a Beverly Hills trophy address?

Trousdale is prized for geometry as much as geography. Developed in the late 1950s on former ranch land, it is an enclave of some 400 flat-pad lots engineered for the one thing Los Angeles hillsides rarely offer: level ground with panoramic, protected views. Strict height and ridgeline rules keep those sightlines open house to house.

The pedigree is architectural, too. The enclave became a canvas for mid-century masters working in low, horizontal volumes calibrated to the pad and the horizon. That lineage is why land here holds value independently of whatever structure happens to sit on it at a given moment.

22,300Square feet of the Trousdale estate now listed, per Canyon News

What does a 22,300-square-foot listing signal for the 2026 market?

It signals that trophy value has migrated from raw square footage toward land, elevation, and permanence. The estate, which Persson reportedly bought in 2014 for a then-record price, is substantial by any measure — but in Trousdale the scarce, durable asset is the view corridor and the pad beneath the house, not the floor area itself.

That distinction matters for how these homes are priced and held. Across the Westside's highest tier, the assets that compound in value are the ones that cannot be rebuilt on demand:

  • The protected, flat-pad view parcel.
  • The address and its architectural provenance.
  • Construction built to outlast the taste cycle, not be replaced by it.

Here is the tension an architect sees in the listing. A 22,300-square-foot contemporary estate is roughly four times the footprint of the restrained mid-century homes that made Trousdale famous — a shift from horizontal discretion toward sheer volume. Whether that scale ages as gracefully as the enclave's original logic is the real question, and it is a design question before it is a market one.

In Trousdale, the land and the view hold the value. The house is the variable.

For the broader LA luxury market, the read is straightforward. Buyers at this level are increasingly underwriting permanence: the premium accrues to homes where site and structure were conceived to endure, and the discount falls on anything that reads as a candidate for the next teardown. The Westside has always rewarded durability of address; in 2026 it is beginning to reward durability of building, too.

So the Persson listing is worth watching less for its headline number than for what buyers decide the house is worth relative to the land it stands on. The answer will tell us how much the market now pays for architecture built to remain — and how much it still treats even a trophy structure as temporary.
